transcript.text: Our client is Peak Performance Sports, a mid-sized chain of 40 sporting goods retail stores across the Midwest. Profits dropped 30% last year even though revenue was roughly flat. The CEO wants to know why, and what to do. How would you approach this?
Before I structure this, a few quick clarifying questions. First, what's the objective exactly -- are we just diagnosing the cause, or also expected to recommend fixes?
Diagnose the driver of the profit decline and recommend actions.
Got it. And is this profit decline specific to Peak Performance, or is the whole industry seeing this?
Good question -- industry is growing about 2%, and competitors' profits are roughly flat. This looks specific to Peak Performance.
Useful, that rules out a pure market-wide explanation. Did the store count or footprint change -- any openings or closures?
No -- all 40 stores were open the full year in both years.

Okay, here's how I'd structure this: since revenue is flat but profit dropped, I want to split this into revenue drivers, cost drivers, and any one-time or external factors. Given revenue is flat, my instinct is this is mostly a margin or cost story rather than a volume story, but I want to check the numbers to confirm rather than assume. Could I see a P&L breakdown?
Sure, here's the breakdown: revenue 198 to 200, COGS 55.1% to 62.0% of revenue, gross profit 44.9% to 38.0%, SG&A 62 to 55, store operating costs flat at 24, net profit 20 to 14.

So gross margin fell about 7 points, that's roughly a $14M hit, way more than explains the full profit drop -- and SG&A actually went down, so this is entirely a margin story, not a cost-control story. I'd want to know what's driving the margin compression -- did pricing, promotions, or product mix change?
Yes to both -- the company ran significantly more discount promotions this year, and there's also been a shift toward lower-margin footwear and away from higher-margin apparel.
That lines up. Can I see the category mix and margins by category?
Apparel went from 40% to 32% of revenue at about 55% margin, footwear went from 35% to 45% at about 28% margin, equipment stayed roughly flat around 40% margin.
That's a meaningful mix shift toward the lowest-margin category. Is there something driving increased discounting specifically -- new competition, maybe?
Yes -- a national online retailer expanded aggressive discounting in the region this year, and Peak Performance matched some of those discounts to stay competitive.

Okay, so to synthesize: revenue held up, but gross margin collapsed from two compounding causes -- a shift in product mix toward lower-margin footwear, and increased discounting to match a new online competitor. My recommendation: first, rebalance product mix back toward higher-margin apparel through merchandising and floor space, rather than let footwear keep growing its share by default. Second, rethink the promotional strategy -- matching an online-only competitor's discounts head-on is a losing game given their lower cost structure, so I'd look at targeted promotions or differentiation on service/experience instead of blanket discount matching. Third, I noticed payroll hours were mentioned as a possible factor -- I'd want to check if that's linked to a service initiative that could support the apparel push, or if it's just cost creep worth trimming. I'd flag as a risk that we may not fully recover to the old margin given the competitor's now a permanent fixture, so I'd want to set a realistic margin recovery target rather than assume full reversion.
That's a good summary of your recommendation. That's all the time we have for this case.
